description: We are a team of students from the San Joaquin Delta College Aerospace Club interested in aerospace, engineering, technology, and problem-solving. Our goal is to work collaboratively, learn from the challenge, and create a practical and creative solution using NASA data and resources. We are excited to combine our different skills and perspectives while gaining hands-on experience through the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary: Little Orbit is a browser-based space mission simulator built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players create a captain, spin for one of eight destinations from Mercury to Neptune with a science objective and a budget, then build a spacecraft by choosing power, batteries, instruments, antennas, propulsion and a launch vehicle. Every choice trades off mass, power, budget, delta-v, data and mission lifetime, and a live dashboard shows each effect as it happens. Players then fly the mission through launch stages such as Max-Q, orbit insertion and the capture burn, handle random emergencies, lead a crew through tasks based on real International Space Station work, and receive a scored mission report that explains why the mission succeeded or failed. The physics, planetary data, launch-window math and mission rules come from NASA, JPL and ESA sources, which we checked item by item in a technical data report. Little Orbit gives students who never get to design a real mission a way to feel the connected trade-offs that real mission teams face, in a game they can finish in one sitting.
details:
Little Orbit: A Space Mission Simulator

▶ WATCH THE GAMEPLAY HERE and PLAY THE GAME!

WHAT IT DOES

Little Orbit is an interactive game that takes a player through a complete space mission, from concept to final report, in five stages:

1. Pilot: Create a captain, choose Easy or Standard mode, and pick a specialty. Engineer makes the spacecraft bus lighter, Scientist boosts instrument value, Pilot widens flight tolerances, and Diplomat halves government budget cuts.

2. Destiny: Spin a mission wheel for one of eight destinations (Mercury, Venus, Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, Europa, Titan, Neptune), a science objective, a mission twist and a starting grant.

3. Build: Drag or tap parts into an assembly bay: solar arrays or a radioisotope generator, batteries, one or two science instruments, an antenna, chemical or electric propulsion, optional extras (radiation vault, thermal blanket, star tracker, backup computer) and a launch vehicle. A mission dashboard tracks budget, launch mass, power demand, delta-v, science potential, downlink capacity and energy reserve in real time. Launch stays locked until the design passes every pre-flight check. While players build, a "funding wire" posts news events, such as government budget cuts, supplier inflation, state co-funding or a university payload offer, that change the grant.

4. Flight: Short interactive stages cover ignition timing, Max-Q (dynamic pressure), power-bus recovery, sensor cross-checks, a debris radar drill, orbit insertion and the capture burn. Random emergencies force quick engineering decisions.

5. Crew and Report: Players walk a six-room crew deck and complete tasks based on real ISS work: replacing a CO2 scrubber filter, tending a VEG-03-style plant garden, securing floating inventory, reading back relay commands and framing science photos. The mission ends with a scored report covering science returned, spacecraft health, piloting accuracy, emergency response and budget discipline. A score of 70 or higher passes, and the report explains why the mission succeeded or failed.

HOW IT WORKS (THE SCIENCE INSIDE)

- The rocket equation (delta-v = Isp x g0 x ln(m0 / m_dry)) runs live, so every kilogram a player adds visibly reduces delta-v.

- Solar output follows the inverse-square law using NASA fact-sheet solar irradiance, so solar power fails at Titan and Neptune and players must switch to nuclear power.

- Launch windows use a Hohmann transfer and Kepler's third law. Our code reproduces JPL's "Let's Go to Mars" lesson: a 259-day trip with Mars 44 degrees ahead of Earth.

- Orbital speed, orbit period and eclipse battery sizing use the standard two-body equations with NASA constants.

- Destination rules follow real missions: a radiation vault at Europa (Europa Clipper), a sunshade at Mercury (MESSENGER), and nuclear power for the outer planets (MMRTG, Dragonfly).

- Budget rules follow NASA practice: the 2026 Small Explorer $190M cost cap, cost reserves, mass and power margins, and environmental testing (shake, thermal-vacuum and radio checks).

We wrote a Little Orbit Technical Data Report that checks every number and formula in the game against 53 published sources. It labels each item as verified, based on real practice, or a game value, and lists where the game simplifies reality.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Most students learn orbits, power, propulsion and budgets as separate topics. Little Orbit puts them in one system, so players see that adding a better instrument raises science but also raises mass, power draw, cost and data volume. There is rarely one perfect design: different combinations of parts, orbits and rockets can reach the same goal. Easy mode makes the game accessible to beginners and younger students, and Standard mode gives full control to students who want more depth. A built-in field manual explains every concept in plain language, a tap-based calculator supports the math problems, and the report teaches why each decision mattered rather than only saying right or wrong. We want students to feel what it is like to design under real engineering limits before they ever join a mission team.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks and no install. It runs in any modern browser on desktop or touch devices.

- HTML Canvas for the walkable crew deck and minigames.

- Adobe Illustrator for slide and promotional graphics.

- Soundtrap for the game soundtrack ("Astronaut Type Beat").

- Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) as SI tools. See our SI disclosure.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Little Orbit mixes a real engineering design loop with arcade-style moments: a mission roulette wheel, a live funding news feed, a debris-shield drill, a walkable pixel-art spacecraft and NPC crewmates with specialties. Every game mechanic is tied to a real trade-off, and the game is honest about which numbers are real and which are simplified.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy vs. playability: Physics, planetary data and mission rules come from NASA, JPL and ESA. Part masses, prices, scores and timers are simplified game values so that a full mission fits in one session, and the game labels them that way.

- Accessibility: Easy and Standard modes, tap and keyboard controls, a pause-able guidebook, and optional paid "assistance" with fees and consequences shown up front.

- Fairness: Budget cuts never push the grant below the cheapest workable design.

- Limits and next steps: Team play is currently one player with NPC crewmates who have roles. Next, we plan shared multiplayer for up to four players, a classroom mode, gravity-assist trajectories, and hardware values tuned closer to NASA's (for example, MMRTG power and ion-engine Isp).
